Toxicology Chapter 199

Hydrocarbons and Volatile Substances

Hydrocarbon questions are usually airway questions wearing a toxicology coat. The dangerous words are coughing, choking, gasping, dyspnea after ingestion, because they imply aspiration chemical pneumonitis. The second board trap is systemic toxicity from aromatic or halogenated hydrocarbons: sudden dysrhythmia, hepatic injury, renal tubular acidosis, carboxyhemoglobinemia, or methemoglobinemia.

Board lens: do not reflexively give charcoal, lavage, prophylactic antibiotics, or steroids. Support oxygenation, avoid preventable aspiration, and call poison control for symptomatic or high-risk compounds.

Products and Exposure Patterns

AliphaticGasoline, kerosene, lamp oil, lighter fluid, mineral spirits. Aspiration risk dominates.
AromaticBenzene, toluene, xylene. Think systemic toxicity and solvent abuse.
HalogenatedCarbon tetrachloride, chloroform, methylene chloride, trichloroethylene. Think dysrhythmia, liver, kidney, delayed COHb.
Abuse routesHuffing rag, bagging plastic bag, sniffing direct inhalation.
Tintinalli Tables 199-1 and 199-2

The source tables separate common household/occupational products from commonly abused volatile agents. Use the product name to predict aspiration versus systemic toxicity.

Pathophysiology

Aspiration physics: low viscosity + low surface tension + high volatility means the liquid spreads easily, vaporizes at body temperature, and reaches distal airways.

Aspiration injures alveolar and capillary membranes and disrupts surfactant, producing chemical pneumonitis, edema, bronchospasm, and sometimes necrotizing pneumonitis or hemorrhagic pulmonary edema.

Systemic toxicity is compound-specific. Halogenated and aromatic hydrocarbons can sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines, causing ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden sniffing death. Toluene can cause renal tubular acidosis with severe hypokalemia. Methylene chloride is metabolized to carbon monoxide, so carboxyhemoglobin may rise late.

Clinical Features

Tintinalli Table 199-3

Pulmonary

Immediate coughing, choking, gasping, dyspnea, mouth burning, tachypnea, wheeze, grunting, or retractions means presume aspiration. Fever can be inflammatory and may appear initially or after 6 to 8 hours.

Radiograph trap: an early CXR can be clear despite symptoms. Changes usually appear within 2 to 6 hours and are almost always present by 24 hours if they occur.

Cardiac and CNS

Ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation is most feared with halogenated and aromatic exposures. CNS effects range from excitement and hallucinations to ataxia, lethargy, coma, and hypoxia-related injury.

Metabolic and Hematologic Clues

Toluene: normal anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, weakness/paralysis; metabolites may also create an anion gap. Methylene chloride: delayed carboxyhemoglobinemia. Amine-containing hydrocarbons: delayed methemoglobinemia. Naphthalene: hemolysis risk.

Treatment

Tintinalli Table 199-4
Airway and breathingOxygen, bronchodilator if bronchospasm, ventilatory support for hypoxemia. Use PEEP/positive pressure thoughtfully because pneumatocele/barotrauma can occur.
CardiacMonitor, ECG, fluids for hypotension. Avoid catecholamines when possible after halogenated/aromatic exposures.
DecontaminationRemove contaminated clothing, soap/cold water skin wash, saline eye irrigation. Protect staff from fumes and additives.
GI deconNo routine lavage or charcoal; both can worsen aspiration risk. Discuss rare high-risk co-ingestions with poison control.
Avoid routine: exogenous catecholamines, prophylactic antibiotics, corticosteroids, activated charcoal, and gastric lavage.

Drug Dose Reference

InterventionUseBoard Notes
Supplemental oxygenHypoxia, aspiration pneumonitis, carboxyhemoglobinemia from methylene chlorideSupportive care is the main treatment.
Inhaled beta-2 agonistBronchospasm after aspirationReasonable; evidence specific to hydrocarbon pneumonitis is limited.
Isotonic crystalloidInitial hypotension/volume supportPreferred before catecholamines when feasible.
Lidocaine, esmolol, or propranololReported options for hydrocarbon-induced ventricular dysrhythmiasConsult poison control/toxicology; avoid QT-prolonging class IA/III agents.
Methylene blueClinically significant methemoglobinemia from amine-containing hydrocarbonsSee dyshemoglobinemia chapter for dosing/contraindications.

Key Points

Symptoms beat filmsEarly normal CXR does not exclude aspiration pneumonitis.
Charcoal trapHydrocarbons adsorb poorly and vomiting/aspiration is the real danger.
Catecholamine trapAromatic/halogenated hydrocarbons can sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines.
Toluene clueGlue/paint exposure plus weakness, hypokalemia, RTA pattern.
DispositionAsymptomatic nonhalogenated aliphatic exposure: observe about 6 to 8 hours, then discharge if still well.
ConsultPoison control for symptoms, aromatic/halogenated agents, toxic additives, or uncertain product.

Inline MCQs

A toddler takes a sip of lamp oil, coughs immediately, then looks well. What is the key early concern?

A. Hydrocarbons mainly threaten the lungs after aspiration, not caustic mucosal necrosis.

B. Coughing/choking after ingestion means presume aspiration risk.

C. Some halogenated compounds can injure liver, but simple lamp oil is mainly aspiration risk.

D. Methemoglobinemia is specific to selected amine-containing agents.

Tintinalli Ch.199: pulmonary toxicity after hydrocarbon aspiration.

Which physical profile creates the highest aspiration risk?

A. This profile tends to flow and spread less.

B. Thin, spreading, volatile liquids move easily across mucosa and vaporize at body temperature.

C. Solids and high-viscosity substances are usually lower aspiration risk.

D. High boiling point means lower volatility.

Tintinalli Ch.199: pathophysiology of aspiration risk.

A solvent user collapses moments after inhaling a halogenated compound. What mechanism is classically feared?

A. Sudden sniffing death is linked to ventricular dysrhythmias from myocardial catecholamine sensitization.

B. Hypocalcemia is not the classic mechanism here.

C. Hydrocarbons are CNS depressants but not opioid agonists.

D. Renal effects can occur with selected solvents but do not explain sudden collapse.

Tintinalli Ch.199: cardiac toxicity and sudden sniffing death.

A young patient with glue sniffing has severe weakness, non-anion gap acidosis, hypokalemia, and urine pH >5.5. Which agent fits best?

A. Toluene abuse can produce renal tubular acidosis with profound hypokalemia and weakness.

B. Methane is an asphyxiant gas, not the classic RTA pattern.

C. Paraffin wax is long-chain/high viscosity.

D. Mineral oil is not the signature cause of this metabolic pattern.

Tintinalli Ch.199: renal and metabolic toxicity from toluene.

Which decontamination step is generally discouraged after isolated hydrocarbon ingestion?

A. This is appropriate for dermal exposure.

B. Eye irrigation is appropriate when exposed.

C. Charcoal adsorbs hydrocarbons poorly and increases vomiting/aspiration risk.

D. Soap-and-water decontamination is standard for skin exposure.

Tintinalli Ch.199: decontamination recommendations.

An asymptomatic child after nonhalogenated aliphatic hydrocarbon ingestion remains well after observation. What disposition is typical?

A. Asymptomatic patients can often go home after 6 to 8 hours if reliable follow-up and return precautions exist.

B. ICU admission is for respiratory compromise or systemic toxicity.

C. Antibiotics are not prophylactic.

D. Steroids have no clear benefit for hydrocarbon pneumonitis.

Tintinalli Ch.199: disposition and follow-up.

A. Early films can be deceptively clear.

B. Radiographic changes may lag; symptomatic aspiration needs observation and supportive care.

C. Charcoal raises aspiration risk.

D. Symptoms mean clinically significant exposure is possible.
